items.author: Mustard
items.content:
<article>Get Nebula for 50% off using my link: https://go.nebula.tv/mustard 

Watch Unsealed Episode 3 here: https://nebula.tv/videos/mustard-the-insane-plan-to-land-airliners-on-aircraft-carriers

Twitter: https://x.com/MustardVideos

In the mid-1950s, as the Cold War intensified, the Soviet Union tested its first true hydrogen bomb, raising the terrifying prospect of a nuclear attack on American soil. The United States had a dangerous weakness: its nuclear bombers sat on predictable airfields, vulnerable to a surprise Soviet strike. If many of America’s bombers were destroyed before they could take off, America could lose its ability to strike back. With its deterrent at risk, the Cold War had entered a dangerous new phase. 

The Navy had an audacious solution: a jet-powered flying boat that could deliver a nuclear strike without ever needing a runway. The Martin P6M SeaMaster would be the centerpiece of what the Navy called the Seaplane Striking Force, a fleet of bombers that would lie in wait, take off from the ocean at a moment’s notice, fly low to evade enemy radar, and strike Soviet targets from the sea. When the order came, these bombers could strike before the Soviets knew it was coming.

But there was a problem. The Navy wasn’t supposed to have its own nuclear bomber fleet. Strategic bombing belonged to the Air Force. Instead, the Navy officially presented the SeaMaster as a high-speed minelayer. Behind the cover story, engineers were working tirelessly to turn an enormous seaplane into a near-supersonic strike aircraft that would rival the Air Force’s B-52. It meant battling punishing ocean conditions, violent vibrations, and a series of dangerous setbacks.

By 1959, the redesigned SeaMaster was closer than ever to becoming operational. But a new threat emerged, and it didn’t come from the Soviet Union.</article>

items.title: Between the czar and Hitler - The forgotten story of the White Army | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>The Russian Civil War was one of the 20th century's bloodiest chapters. The fight for Russia between Lenin's Red Army and the White Army was ruthless. Its legacy can be felt in Europe to this day.

Nestled in the Alps in Austrian East Tyrol, a cemetery bears witness to a dark chapter in European history. In 1945, following 27 years of war, flight and survival, the White Army's long journey came to a tragic end there.

Russia, 1917: Czar Nicholas II was forced to abdicate, bringing 300 years of Romanov rule to an end. Lenin and his wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, returned from exile in Switzerland determined to reshape the country according to their vision. But alongside the Bolsheviks, Lenin's radical communist followers, another force emerged to claim Russia: The White Army.

The White Army was made up largely of generals and officers from the former czarist armed forces, who openly opposed the Communists. Women were also among its ranks — including Maria Bochkareva, who commanded the famous Women's Battalion of the White Army. Until 1922, the Red and White armies waged a brutal struggle for the control of Russia.

After its defeat, the White Army fled to the Balkans, while many other supporters of the czar scattered across Europe. Paris filled with Russians driven into exile. Former princesses often made their living as art models — they saw no future in a country ruled by the Red Army.

When Hitler invaded the Soviet Union, former White Army soldiers saw another chance to fight the hated Bolsheviks. Many openly sympathized with Nazi Germany, viewing it as a defense against Stalin.

By the end of World War II, the White Army was left confronting its own ruined hopes for a Russia liberated from Bolshevik rule.

This documentary traces the history of the White Army and explores a little-known chapter of European history — one that spans revolution, exile and political radicalization.

items.author: Bloomberg Originals

<article>A year after becoming Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi is pursuing an ambitious plan to build a stronger, richer and more secure country. At the center of her strategy is a target of ¥370 trillion ($2.3 trillion) in public and private investment, spanning artificial intelligence, semiconductors, defense, energy, food technology and even manga.

But as Takaichi enters her second year in power, Japan faces a formidable combination of pressures: a weak yen, rising living costs, a shrinking workforce, enormous government debt and worsening relations with China. Takaichi also wants Japan to spend more on defense as security challenges grow across Asia.

This documentary examines Takaichi’s first year as prime minister, the forces that brought her to power and the risks surrounding her agenda.

items.title: Open Source Is Under Attack & AI Made It Worse • Steve Poole & Olimpiu Pop • GOTO 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for GOTO Unscripted. #GOTOcon #GOTOunscripted
https://gotopia.tech

Steve Poole - Developer Advocate at HeroDevs & Community Director at London Java Community
Olimpiu Pop - Technologist & Tech Journalist

Check out more here:
https://gotopia.tech/articles/457

RESOURCES
Steve
https://x.com/spoole167
https://github.com/spoole167
https://www.linkedin.com/in/noregressions

Olimpiu
https://x.com/olimpiupop
https://github.com/zroll
https://www.linkedin.com/in/olimpiupop

DESCRIPTION
Steve Poole of HeroDevs, a longtime voice on software supply chain security, tells host Olimpiu Pop that the landscape has hit a "watershed moment" in the last few weeks. The long-standing attack methods are simple: typo'd or confusingly named packages, unchecked scripts, inflated version numbers that trick builds into pulling the wrong release, and maintainers who build trust and then turn bad. Developers are among the weakest links because their machines hold so many credentials. The new factor is AI-driven vulnerability discovery, which both attackers and security researchers are using. Steve's concern is that discovery is now industrialized while fixing is not: maintainers who once saw a CVE or two a year may now face batches of them, and he fears more will simply walk away. Unsupported packages are especially exposed, since CVEs against them often never get reported at all. His worst-case scenario is that open source security fixes end up arriving in small commercial enclaves first, as regulation and cyber insurers push companies to pay for maintenance.

The practical advice for engineers is concrete. Fixing an open source dependency yourself is fine once, but then CVEs two through six arrive and you are in the maintenance business. Instead, scrutinize and reduce your dependencies, noting that studies suggest AI-generated apps pick roughly three times more of them than people do. Stay as close to HEAD as you can on maintained releases, and build your pipelines into "sleek engines" that can upgrade continuously, because under the EU Cyber Resilience Act "best efforts" to fix a vulnerability will not mean a migration in six months (Steve is clear he is not a lawyer). The two close on responsibility: like a compiler's output, AI-generated code is still your code, as Kubernetes' AI policy makes explicit by ruling out AI co-authorship. The hard part is the non-deterministic output, which means thinking harder about testing and proving quality. Steve's closing hope is that the industry becomes more pragmatic about AI's downsides, though he admits so many forces are converging that it's hard to predict where this ends.

items.title: The shingles vaccine could be a tool to prevent Alzheimer’s
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Scientists may have found an unexpected clue in the fight against Alzheimer’s: the shingles vaccine. When researchers compared people born just days apart — where one group was eligible for the vaccine and the other wasn’t — those who got it seemed less likely to develop Alzheimer’s. Nobody is sure why. It might calm chronic inflammation, or give an aging immune system a boost. But it’s one more sign that we’re still trying to solve a disease we don’t fully understand. #Unexplainable

items.title: Killing time - The science of boredom | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Our modern lives are wired for productivity, speed and constant stimulation. Boredom? No time! Yet boredom can fire up our creativity and help teach us to manage our emotions.

In a world built for productivity, speed and nonstop stimulation, it seems there's little room left for boredom. Smartphones offer us endless distraction, making it easy to avoid the uncomfortable feeling. But what actually is boredom? And why do we feel it? Everybody experiences boredom, yet few of us take it seriously. Researchers around the world are working to better understand it — because beneath that nagging sense of emptiness lies far more than most people realize.

The documentary is an entertaining exploration of how boredom can be not only unpleasant — but also beneficial. Feeling bored encourages us to look for ways out of dull situations and can help boost our creativity. It also plays an important role in childhood, as we learn to manage our emotions. Researchers do caution against idealizing boredom, though. When it becomes chronic, it can contribute to problems such as alcoholism, and internet and gambling addictions.

We all know boredom — yet we all experience it differently. Is it an agonizing emptiness, or a driving force behind creativity? Nervous restlessness, or restful calm? In fascinating experiments, researchers in psychology, neuroscience and philosophy explore this elusive feeling. How can some people tolerate boredom better than others? How much boredom is healthy — and what actually happens in the brain when nothing is happening? Spoiler: Quite a lot!

items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>The Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status for hundreds of thousands of Haitians who had fled violence and upheaval, saying that Haiti was now safe enough for them to return home. What is the reality on the ground in Haiti?

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

“Haiti Deportation Crisis” offers a rare, up-close look at the extent and impact of gang violence in Haiti, the efforts to combat it, and the rising fears among Haitians in the U.S. of being sent back.
  
In vivid detail, the documentary shows how armed gangs now control large parts of Haiti, how massacres and mass kidnappings are devastating families, and how efforts to stem the violence are playing out so far — including the work of the Gang Suppression Force, a newly-established international military mission backed by the U.N. and 18 countries including the U.S.

Unfolding against the backdrop of the end of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians, what emerges is a visceral documentation of life inside a country many Haitians in the U.S. say is as dangerous as ever  — and where they fear they’ll be kidnapped, ransomed, or killed if they’re deported. The documentary also examines how the end of TPS is impacting communities in the U.S. with large Haitian populations, such as Springfield, Ohio.

items.title: The Complete Story Of The Assassination Of JFK: Minute-By-Minute
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>On November 22, 1963, President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dealey Plaza, Dallas, Texas. While the Warren Commission concluded that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone, decades of ballistic analysis, witness statements, and forensic studies suggest a far more complex conspiracy. From the Mafia and Jimmy Hoffa to Soviet agents and segregationists, JFK had powerful enemies. items.title: In the shadow of copper - The price of mining in Serbia | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>The small Serbian town of Bor lives from copper mining. Many residents say that high levels of pollution from the mine, which has been majority-owned by a Chinese corporation since 2018, are making them sick.

Resistance is growing in the town Bor in eastern Serbian. Lazar Milutinovic and Marko Andrejevic are members of the student movement that has been driving social change in Serbia for more than two years. Meanwhile, others point to the high levels of heavy metal contamination measured in the area, the high incidence of cancer and the low life expectancy.

Environmental engineer Snezana Serbula has spent her entire professional career investigating the mine’s impact on Bor. One of Serbia’s most prominent critics of mining, she has published numerous scientific studies on the effects of heavy metal emissions on the environment and on human health.

In this report, workers say they were not adequately informed about the possible long-term consequences of mining. Meanwhile, local residents accuse the authorities and the company of a lack of transparency. Lazar and Marko have founded an opposition movement in the town, calling for greater oversight and stricter environmental regulations.

Jasna Tomic lives in the village of Krivelj near Bor. She could soon lose her home: The village, which has been inhabited by the Vlach ethnic minority for centuries, is expected to make way for the mine. Many of her neighbors have already left. Jasna fears she, too, will soon have to relocate. She is fighting to ensure that the village community can at least find a new home together.

items.title: Is Chemistry the Same Throughout the Universe? With Kate the Chemist
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>Would aliens use the same periodic table as us? Neil deGrasse Tyson and comic co-host Negin Farsad sit down with Kate Biberdorf, aka Kate the Chemist, to tackle fan questions about the chemistry of life, diamonds, how fire works, and spontaneous combustion.

Is there such a thing as a liquid diamond and could you swim in a pool of it? Kate walks through the phase chemistry of carbon, why melting a diamond means it's no longer a diamond, and what the difference actually is between a crystal and a liquid crystal. Do crystals actually influence energy? We discuss crystal shops, the science behind why crystals are the lowest energy state of their atoms, and why "diamonds are forever" is really just a statement about molecular stability.

Could life on other planets be built from completely different chemistry? Kate and Neil explore silicon as a carbon alternative, the case for methane as a solvent on Titan, amino acids found on asteroids, and the biggest open question in astrobiology: is DNA inevitable, or just one solution among many that the universe stumbled upon? Would intelligent aliens organize a periodic table the same way we do or could they sort by stability, conductivity, or cosmic abundance instead?

What is the fire triangle? Learn about the chemistry of fire and the lesser-known Pentagon of dust explosions, explaining how sugar factory explosions happen. We discuss ATP in the body and its role in transferring and storing energy. The episode closes on a series of spectacular chemistry demonstrations — dry ice vortex pools, exploding paint cans, acid base reactions with glitter and food coloring — and Kate's upcoming live science stage tour. items.title: 1750-1900: Exploring The Industrial Revolution's Most Important Sites
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>From Big Pit's dark shafts to Canary Wharf's glass towers, Britain’s landscape tells a radical story. Fly above the clues carved by coal, cotton, steam and steel.

Join historian Dr Alex Langlands on a south Wales flight path to the valleys where open-cast scars and towering spoil heaps fueled a steam-powered leap forward. Meet retired miner Kerry Thompson as he recalls camaraderie 90 metres down and the dangers that shadowed every shift. Then track Isambard Kingdom Brunel’s ambition from the Clifton Suspension Bridge to the Great Western Railway, a vision that stitched mines, mills and ports together. In Manchester’s Cottonopolis, discover why rivers, damp air, and a freewheeling oligarchy supercharged textile mills run by women and children. Step into back-to-back housing, wake-week escapes to Blackpool Tower’s ballroom, and the precarious present at Port Talbot. Finally, see how derelict Docklands became Canary Wharf.

This is the Industrial Revolution written onto the land - and still shaping lives today. Watch to uncover the surprising links you can only see from above.

<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub

https://ash-hq.org

DESCRIPTION
Rebecca Le and Zach Daniel, co-authors of "Ash Framework: Create Declarative Elixir Web Apps" and maintainers of the framework, tell host Christian Alexander how the book came to be: Rebecca wanted to write the guide she wished she'd had when learning Ash, where all the pieces existed but it wasn't clear how they fit together. The book builds a music-database app (Tunez) in small steps and adds authentication, policies, and testing at the point a real project would need them, rather than front-loading the hardest material. The surprising conclusion is that writing it changed the framework. Ash had deliberately offered no testing guidance, but when Zach tried to explain how to test, he found it couldn't be explained as things stood, so they built the generator-based testing support that now ships with Ash. Zach also describes the framework's core bet as extensibility: where Rails is "omakase," Ash is a Chipotle bowl, with extensions (event sourcing, TypeScript bindings, Ash AI) that can reshape how everything works, which is why the book's foundational concepts have stayed stable even as the ecosystem moved quickly.

For engineers weighing a framework, the discussion offers a few concrete takeaways. Ash's learning curve is steep up front but flattens: once you know resources, actions, and policies, hard problems like APIs, authentication internals, and nested forms reuse the same concepts. Zach recalls a client whose API layer ended up as a single line of code, though he's candid that a line that powerful has to be understood (hence his lightsaber analogy). Rebecca built the first version of the Cinder data table library in about a week, and Zach's team at Remedy replaced a half-baked in-house version with it and deleted a large amount of code. Finally, Zach reports that AI has made the up-front cost much easier to absorb: at his company, engineers who had never learned Elixir are delivering on an Ash project in under three weeks, and basic "I got this error" questions have nearly disappeared from the community Discord.

items.title: 4,000 Years Of British History In 25 Minutes
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>From the cockpit, forgotten stories appear in plain sight. Historian-pilot Dr. Ben Robinson spots traces most of us miss—and they change how you see Britain.

Glide over Halvergate Marshes to discover how medieval peat digging accidentally birthed the Norfolk Broads, then meet the last great survivor of the trading fleet—the Albion wherry with its once-blackened sails. A ruined abbey hides monastic fish ponds designed to impress, while Chatsworth House reveals Capability Brown’s radical makeover that rewrote garden fashion. The camera lifts the veil on the Enclosure Acts and Highland Clearances through the haunting survival of Oakendrain, and jumps to Ireland’s potato blight to show how hunger reshaped fields. Finally, step inside Cornwall’s Eden Project, where vast biomes rise from an old clay pit to model a different future for land and climate.

Take the full flight to see how rivers, gardens, laws, and livelihoods carved a “green and pleasant land”—and what its next chapter might be. Watch now to uncover the clues written across the British landscape from above.

#NorfolkBroads #BenRobinson #BritishLandscape #AerialArchaeology #CapabilityBrown #EdenProject #HistoryDocumentary #EuropeFromAbove</article>

items.title: One electric truck's road trip to Norway | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Trucker Tobias Wagner's mission: to get from Germany's East Frisia to Norway in an electric truck. A navigation buoy from the Juister Riff in the North Sea went missing and has turned up in Scandinavia. Now, it's Wagner's job to bring it back.

Tackling 900 kilometers, three countries and a ferry crossing — all in an electric truck. To make the trip work, Wagner has had to plan his route carefully. Weight, distance and road incline all affect the truck's range. Finding suitable overnight stops is also crucial, since not all truck parking areas have charging stations.

Many in his industry are still skeptical about electric trucks. But freight hauler Nanno Janssen has no doubt: e-trucks are the future. Sixty percent of his fleet already runs on electricity, and he plans to transition the remaining trucks in the coming years. Tobias Wagner is a believer, too. He regularly shares his experiences as "Elektrotrucker" on YouTube.

The film follows Wagner on this unusual assignment. It shows how today's electric mobility is already working for long-haul trucking — and looks at the challenges that remain.

items.title: Mao Zedong and China's Cultural Revolution (3/3) | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>From peasants' son to revolutionary leader — Mao Zedong laid the foundation for modern China. This three-part documentary offers an in-depth look at one of the most influential figures of the 20th century.

The legacy of the "founding father" of the People's Republic of China remains deeply controversial. Revered in Europe as a revolutionary icon in the late 1960s, Mao led China to the brink of disaster and ultimately clung to power with a regime of terror. Yet today's leaders in Beijing continue to draw on the cult of Mao. China is now a global power, a transformation that would be difficult to imagine without Mao Zedong.

When Mao Zedong was born in 1893, nothing hinted at his meteoric rise to power. The son of a farming family, he grew up during a period of political instability and profound social upheaval. The 1911 Revolution, which marked the beginning of the end of imperial rule, awakened his mind to politics. At first, Mao had no clear political program. But the Russian Revolution of 1917 introduced him to Marxist ideas, and he soon became a co-founder of the Communist Party of China.

Mao rose steadily through the party ranks as conflict with the nationalist Kuomintang party intensified into a bloody civil war. The devastating retreat that became known as the "Long March" went down in history to become the foundation of the cult of Mao. After World War II, the struggle for power in China continued until Mao and his forces finally reached Beijing.

This three-part series traces Mao Zedong's journey from peasants' son to revolutionary and architect of modern China — from his rural childhood to the founding of the People's Republic to the devastating impact of the Cultural Revolution in the 1960s, which claimed millions of lives.

Archival footage, as well as interviews with historians and eyewitnesses, tell the story of the man who changed China forever.

items.author: Great Art Explained
items.content:
<article>My book Great Art Explained is ready to order now worldwide 
US - https://a.co/d/52C1D6c
UK - https://amzn.eu/d/6EoTxjs

My new Podcast can be found here! https://lnk.bio/primoandpayne

Today Henri Matisse’s the red studio is considered one of the landmarks of modern art, seen by thousands of visitors at the Museum of Modern art in New York. 
But before arriving there in 1948 it spent more than a decade hanging in a London nightclub.

When Matisse painted the red studio in 1911 it was one of the strangest pictures anyone had ever seen - a room almost completely consumed by red – furniture reduced to outlines, paintings hanging on walls that barely seem to exist, and a grandfather clock with 12 numbers but no hands. Even Matisse wasn't entirely sure what he had created and nobody wanted to buy it.

So how did a painting that even its creator struggle to understand, go from rejection and obscurity to becoming a masterpiece of modern art and what was it doing in a London nightclub in the first place?

items.title: The housing crisis in Los Angeles - Between homelessness and luxury real estate | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Los Angeles' housing crisis is escalating dramatically. Those who can't find a place to live have to get creative — otherwise, survival becomes a daily struggle.

Even before the devastating fires of January 2025, affordable housing was in short supply in Los Angeles. Even people earning an average full-time salary are at risk of ending up on the streets. In 2024, the number of homeless people in Los Angeles County was well over 75,000. The chronic housing shortage is driving residents to get creative, while also giving rise to new business ideas: Gregory sells camper vans to working people who can't afford to rent an apartment. He came up with the idea after he himself had to live in a camper van for a while. Car mechanic Roy also lives in a mobile home. The 64-year-old has to supplement his modest pension by working at an auto repair shop.

Since 2012, Elvina, who immigrated to the US, has been renting out beds in large communal dorms for 55 dollars a night. It's a popular solution, and many long-term residents enjoy the social atmosphere. Elvina now operates seven of these facilities throughout California. Meanwhile Shelton, a real estate agent, is living a picture-perfect American dream. She sells luxury homes and lives with her husband and children in the upscale Brentwood neighborhood. It took more than just hard work to achieve her success: the 42-year-old also had to overcome her alcohol addiction. James has now made it off the streets after living for a time in the notorious Skid Row district in the heart of downtown L.A. He wants to give something back, so once a week he offers free haircuts to those who need them. This documentary looks at varying lifestyles and living conditions in a city where the gap between rich and poor is growing ever wider.

items.title: Your location isn’t private | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Why do data brokers have your location data? And what do they use it for? 

One big reason is advertising. Data brokers collect location data from people around the world and sell it to advertising companies who use it to create highly targeted ads.  

This data comes from everyday apps on your phone, like maps, games, dating apps, and weather apps. The apps often collect this information to improve their services, but it can also end up in a global network of data brokers.  

One main issue is that this data can be extremely detailed, showing where people live, work, and spend their free time. With this information, discerning a person's identity can be surprisingly easy, which can pose a serious security risk. 

Although the trade in location data is regulated in certain places, like the EU, advertising companies and data brokers still find ways to access and use citizens' personal data.

items.title: The Global North taken to court - Who pays for the climate catastrophe? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>From their lecture halls to the International Court of Justice. Law students from the South Pacific have joined island nations to demand greater climate accountability from industrialized countries.

The case before the world's highest court was initiated by 27 law students at the University of the South Pacific, all from islands that could become uninhabitable as sea levels rise and storms grow more frequent.

As might be expected, the Global North has pushed back against their demands for greater responsibility for the consequences of climate change. The United States and Germany argue that international climate law doesn't clearly make countries responsible for past emissions. The young law students are going up against opponents who know the international stage inside and out. What gives them the courage and determination to keep going?

In 2023 they achieved an early victory: their campaign for climate justice won the support of the U.N. General Assembly. That lead to a resolution calling for the international community to take action on climate change.

We follow Vishal from Fiji and Jule from Germany. Both are fighting for justice and compensation for climate-related damage in developing countries. Their journey takes them into the world of international diplomacy, where they confront powerful opponents — among them industrialized nations and oil companies who don't want to have to pay out billions in reparations. All the while, lobbyists and diplomats from major nations try to sway the voices of small island states.

The film captures the optimism of these young people who, full of determination and hope, demand accountability on behalf of the generations to come. Exclusive interviews with judges and historical footage highlight the importance of the case. In July 2025, it all culminates in an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice.

items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, how are voters FRONTLINE has been following since 2020 feeling about the direction of the country?

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

Over the past six years, a team of filmmakers has been following more than a dozen Americans — from a doctor to a pastor to a barber to a construction company owner to a retiree — in eight states across the U.S. 

A month before the midterms, how are these Americans feeling about changes in the country and in their own lives?

Their diverse views and experiences unfold in “American Voices 2026,” a 90-minute FRONTLINE documentary that offers a meaningful look at both what unites and divides the U.S. electorate as the midterms approach.

From a team led by award-winning filmmaker Mike Shum, “American Voices 2026” is the latest installment of a unique filmmaking effort begun in 2020. That’s when Shum and FRONTLINE started documenting the lives of voters with differing viewpoints as they navigated a year of extraordinary tumult, from the pandemic to protests to the polls, in the documentary “American Voices: A Nation in Turmoil.” Four years later, “American Voices 2024” chronicled how their hopes and fears had changed since 2020.

Now, “American Voices 2026” explores how their perspectives have evolved amid another polarizing election season, a faltering economy, and a war with Iran that’s now in its eighth month.

Filmed in locations ranging from the Austin, Texas area, to Hayward, California; from Minneapolis, Minnesota, to Beaverdam, Virginia; and from Portland, Oregon, to Sioux City, Iowa, “American Voices 2026” is a journey across geography, race and politics that illuminates where our country has been — and where it is headed.

items.title: Inside RFK's Assassination: Minute-By-Minute
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>Eight shots in a crowded kitchen corridor. A fallen frontrunner. And questions that never faded.

On June 5, 1968, Robert F. Kennedy was shot at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles moments after a primary-night speech. This episode traces the path to that midnight chaos: RFK’s war on Jimmy Hoffa and the Mafia, clashes with J. Edgar Hoover, his civil rights crusade, and a Portland synagogue speech urging stronger US support for Israel that sparked fierce backlash. Inside the pantry, we revisit Sirhan Sirhan’s .22 revolver, the eyewitness confusion, and the forensic riddle of a fatal shot behind the left ear. Why did the official record remain so thin? What fueled rumors of a second gunman? And how did a trial, a commuted sentence, and years of denied parole leave lingering doubts?

Watch to follow the timeline, hear the key voices, and explore the evidence that still divides historians and investigators without giving away the conclusions. Stay to decide for yourself.

#RFK #RobertKennedy #SirhanSirhan #Assassination #History #ColdCase #1968</article>

items.title: How We’ll Get to Alpha-Centauri | Cosmic Queries #115
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>If the multiverse exists, where does our universe end and another begin? Neil deGrasse Tyson and comic co-host Chuck Nice tackle a wide-ranging grab bag of fan questions covering bubble universes, the nature of now, fractals, Hoag's Object, and more.

How do we tell when our universe ends and another begins? We explore the bubble universe model, where separate universes expand without overlapping, each potentially operating under different laws of physics. How can we test for another universe impinging on ours? Next we cover Neil’s favorite and least favorite astronomical words. Could Project Starshot's laser-propelled nanocraft reach Alpha Centauri before a more advanced mission launched decades later? Neil breaks down the math and how lightsails could be our most efficient way of accessing other star systems. 

Is there such a thing as a shared "now"? How does a rubber sheet visualization of gravity actually work in four dimensions? We discuss Hoag’s Object and how calculating chance alignments helped us discover binary star systems. Are fractals the key to understanding everything in the universe or are they more entertaining than useful? How does an expanding universe affect time? Did time pass differently in the past? Plus, what did the sky look like when the cosmic microwave background was visible light?

items.title: France vs Germany: The Culinary Border That Shaped Europe
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>From the golden wheat of Champagne-Ardennes to a monk-run brewhouse on the Danube, Europe’s food map looks different from above. What hidden borders shape how France and Germany eat and drink?

Soar over chalky fields where wheat and barley once rivaled hardy rye, then drop into Schwante to meet master baker Karl Dietmar and his award-winning Roggenmischbrot. Follow the hops to Weltenburg Abbey, where Brother Thomas Freyhardt and brewmaster Ludwig Mederer uphold the Reinheitsgebot in cellars carved centuries ago. Head north to Germany’s edge-of-the-climate vineyards with Dörte Nacken tending Pinot Noir beside an 11th-century monastery, before arriving south of Épernay at a famed walled parcel cherished by the Krug family, where Olivier Krug reveals a vision first written in 1848. Along the way: 275,000 tiny Champagne parcels, exploding bottles, and a trade route that turned bubbles into European history.

If you think bread is French and beer is German, this aerial journey will change your map. Watch to discover the surprising ties that still shape landscapes, tastes, and traditions today. #Champagne #GermanBeer #RyeBread #WineHistory #AerialDocumentary #Europe #FoodHistory</article>

items.title: How Iran survives - Defectors expose the secret apparatus
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>How do you make a soldier shoot at unarmed protestors? Iran's regime has spent 40 years perfecting the answer. In this DW investigation, two high-ranking defectors expose the brutal system of repression.

"No one says: shoot. The order is: stop the protest. How you do it — is up to you."  
Two high-ranking defectors — a former intelligence officer and a commander in Iran's elite special forces — went on the record. Using burner phones, encrypted apps and code words, DW's investigative unit spent months verifying their identities and the documents, photos and footage they shared. 
They reveal secret command centers activated during protests, a clandestine circle of officers responsible for ordering extrajudicial killings — and a system of total control that reaches into the private lives of those who serve it. 
Both men say they have been handed death sentences in absentia. 
This is the story they are risking their lives to tell. 
 
An investigation by Naomi Conrad, Birgitta Schülke and Farzane Saeedi

items.title: The Dolomites - Summer in the Italian Alps | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>From rugged peaks to gentle valleys, Italy's Dolomites are idyllic. In this film, nature lovers show us their mountain world and share fascinating stories about life between tradition and modernity.

In the Dolomites, Italy's "dolce vita" culture meets Alpine tradition — the perfect combination for anyone who wants spectacular natural scenery coupled with a diverse culinary scene. Beyond better-known tourist destinations like Seiser Alm, the Tre Cime di Lavaredo and the Rosengarten, there is much to discover in the Dolomites — or "pale mountains". In the Friulian Dolomites Nature Park, a team of biologists, veterinarians and animal rangers saves the life of an ibex by performing emergency surgery on a crooked horn. 

South of Bolzano, a photographer captures the portraits of elderly mountain farmers and alpinists from remote valleys as part of a UNESCO project — using camera technology that's over a century old. A young shepherd couple spends their summer on a secluded high pasture near the Valles Pass, relishing their modest Alpine lifestyle. An entrepreneur from Trento, a city on the Adige River, makes speaker cabinets from the wood of trees felled by a hurricane, while investing in local reforestation. And in Val Gardena, on one of the oldest farms in the Alps, a family offers guests a menu of traditional Ladin food — the regional cuisine — made with ingredients they grow themselves.

items.title: Why We Haven’t Reached Superintelligence, with David Krakauer
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>Why did intelligence evolve in the universe? Neil deGrasse Tyson, Chuck Nice, and Gary O’Reilly explore the nature of intelligence, information theory, consciousness, and whether AI is actually intelligent at all with David Krakauer, evolutionary biologist and president of the Santa Fe Institute.

Can you conceive of life without intelligence, or intelligence without life? We parse the difference between intelligence and being alive and whether you can be one without the other. What does it mean for something to be called intelligent? Is a bacterium more intelligent than a human that’s actively destroying their own environment? We explore collective intelligence, the difference between signalling and language, and how humans communicate is wholly different from how animals do.

What is the difference between intelligence and consciousness? We discuss unconscious problem solving, expertise, improv comedy, and Srinivasa Ramanujan's mathematical visions. Why do some ideas “just come to us” outside of our inner monologue?  How does AI solve problems differently than us? Are AI tools complementary to human intelligence or competitive with it? We discuss the risk of offloading our capabilities to LLMs run by big companies. What do we lose when we outsource our cognitive tools entirely, and how many generations before that loss becomes irreversible? 

Will tools like LLM ever help humanity solve the biggest mysteries in the universe? Is human cognition too limited to solve the problems we want to solve? We get into information theory and how human intelligence intersects with entropy. How are companies in the AI Revolution doing to information what we did with energy in the Industrial Revolution? We discuss whether superintelligence is possible and how natural selection may only result in a certain types of intelligence. Plus, why did we evolve past bacteria anyway? It’s worked out pretty well for them…

items.title: Systems Programming with Zig • Garrison Hinson-Hasty & Trevor Berrange Sanchez • GOTO 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub
http://gotopia.tech/bookclub

Check out more here:
https://gotopia.tech/episodes/455

Garrison Hinson-Hasty - Author of "Systems Programming with Zig" & Contributor to the Zig Compiler
Trevor Berrange Sanchez - Systems Software Engineer & Particularly Fond of Zig

RESOURCES
Garrison
https://github.com/garrisonhh

Trevor
https://www.linkedin.com/in/trevor-berrange-sanchez-035259426

Links
https://youtu.be/YXrb-DqsBNU
https://youtu.be/wFlyUzUVFhw
https://youtu.be/jIZpKpLCOiU

DESCRIPTION
Garrison Hinson-Hasty, author of “Systems Programming with Zig” and a contributor to the Zig compiler, joins Trevor Berrange Sanchez to explain why he wrote a book on a pre-1.0 language that breaks frequently (he's currently updating the last seven chapters for Zig 0.16). His answer: the language's slow march toward 1.0 is a feature, and learning it now teaches you why its decisions stick. The conversation's core thesis is that Zig is countercultural: instead of stacking new abstractions on old ones, it reuses well-tested ideas and "never adds too much”. "Simple", in the Zig community's sense, means simple relative to what the machine is doing, with integer and pointer types that map closely to how you'd think about data in assembly. Chapter 6's CHIP-8 interpreter shows this: a few integers, some buffers, and elegant results. The same philosophy explains Zig's missing string type. Strings are just byte sequences with a length, and the language leaves encoding choices to you. Garrison notes that Rust, by contrast, now has to maintain its many string types forever.

Two practical takeaways for working engineers. First, allocators: because Zig encourages flat, data-oriented design, the book barely needs dynamic allocation, and when it does, allocators let you reason about memory for a whole phase of a program (say, a compiler's parser) as one unit rather than tracking the lifetime of every AST node. Second, C interop: you can use a C header directly, keep defer for cleanup instead of goto, and write small Zig wrappers around awkward C error-return conventions. The chapter on graphics and OpenGL, meanwhile, is really about a transferable systems skill: working out what an unfamiliar, committee-designed API wants from you when no tutorial exists.

items.title: The Climate Paradox: Why New York City Is Greener Than You Think
items.author: PBS
items.content:
<article>Many people see New York City as an environmental problem. Experts argue the opposite: New Yorkers use less energy, drive less, and have smaller carbon footprints than most Americans. But as Superstorm Sandy revealed, coastal cities like NYC may face some of climate change's greatest dangers.

This excerpt comes from "The Future of Cities" and installment of "New York: A Documentary Film". items.title: How Robert the Bruce Humiliated England | Battle of Bannockburn 1314
items.author: History Hit
items.content:
<article>Take a deep dive into the story of one of the most decisive battles in medieval history.

In 1314, a massive English army headed into Scotland, led by King Edward II. He was on a mission to crush his arch enemy, the Scottish King, Robert the Bruce.

The battle that followed, by the Bannock Burn, was a bloodbath that saw the river run red with English blood.  It has been recounted over the centuries, from poems and songs to movies like ‘Braveheart’.

Historian Helen Carr investigates the evidence around the battle: walking the ground to see just how it unfolded in the Scottish landscape and looking at 700 year old documents in the archives that reveal the triumph of the Bruce and the cataclysmic consequences for Edward II. Join us in a fascinating in-depth exploration of a battle that shaped frontiers and the fortunes of kings.

items.title: We Finally Know More About Humanity’s First Civilization
items.author: Kurzgesagt – In a Nutshell
items.content:
<article>IT’S HERE! The 12,027 Calendar just dropped on the kurzgesagt shop: https://shop.kgs.link/calendar27, and we’re so excited for you to see it. Get yours here, support everything we do, and give your walls a year of stunning kurzgesagt art.

What we know about human history is only a fraction of the full story. Much of the rest is like dark matter, invisible to us. We can’t see it, and we can only see the effects of its presence. But thanks to new techniques for DNA sequencing, dating ancient detritus, mathematical models, and aerial and lidar archaeology, we are now able to get a faint idea of what this world might have looked and felt like.

Who was the first human? Where did the first civilization begin and what did life look like back then?

items.title: How the World Reacted as Global Warming Warnings Grew | Heat (full documentary) | FRONTLINE (PBS)
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>When the threat of climate change emerged as a major global issue, how did some of the world's largest governments and corporations respond? (Aired 2008)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate


Melting glaciers, rising sea levels, fires, floods and droughts: In 2008, with public concern about global warming on the upswing, award-winning producer and correspondent Martin Smith traveled the planet to investigate the scale of the problem, and the scale of any solution.

For years, the film reported, big businesses in the U.S. and around the globe — from oil and coal companies to electric utilities to car manufacturers — had resisted change to environmental policy and stifled the debate over climate change. But as this 2008 documentary was being made, industries and governments were facing rising pressure to reshape their approach to the environment.


To make “Heat,” Smith traveled to 12 countries on four continents, sitting down with policymakers, scientists, and leading executives from many of the largest carbon emitters from around the world, including American oil giants, Chinese coal companies, and Indian SUV makers. 


The two-hour film documented where the political and economic conversation around climate change and global warming stood in 2008, and found that some businesses were trying to fend off new regulations, while others were repositioning themselves to prosper in a world reshaped by climate change. The investigation also found that despite increasing talk about “going green,” environmental concerns were often still taking a back seat to shorter-term economic interests. And there were serious questions about the ability of industry-proposed solutions like “clean coal,” ethanol fuel subsidies, and carbon capture technology to roll back global warming. 


Editor’s note: A line of narration in this documentary cited a since-retracted assertion from the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change that "80 percent of all glacier ice in Tibet and the Himalayas will be gone by 2035." The panel attributed the statement to a media interview with a scientist who later said he had been misquoted, though the IPCC stood by its overall conclusion that “widespread mass loss from glaciers … are projected to accelerate throughout the 21st Century.”

items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>Get an exclusive 15% discount on Saily data plans! Use code BOYLE at checkout. Download Saily app or go to https://www.saily.com/boyle

In September 2026, Turkey's investment fund industry collapsed, after funds run by Tera and Pusula failed to meet redemptions and regulators froze and liquidated 131 funds holding about $20 billion of savings belonging to more than 455,000 investors. In this video, Patrick Boyle looks at how Emre Tezmen's Tera, which hoped to become "the Goldman Sachs of Turkey," reported returns of more than 66,000%, how funds buying thinly traded Borsa Istanbul stocks allegedly inflated their own valuations, and how money market funds that savers treated as cash ended up exposed to inflated shares through reverse repo loans. We also cover the warnings from MSCI and Turkey's finance minister, the arrests and political fallout from what Turkey's justice minister has called "Ponzi-like schemes," what Bernie Cornfeld's Investors Overseas Services and Bill Hwang's Archegos Capital tell us about market manipulation and leverage, and why weak institutions and tiny fines let bad actors drive out honest businesses. Along the way, we try to track down the "notorious malevolent forces" that Tezmen blamed for the collapse.

items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>Millions of Americans have fallen victim to a growing epidemic of online scams — from sextortion schemes aimed at teens, to crypto investment scams targeting seniors. What’s behind the rise?

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

FRONTLINE and The Associated Press have spent more than a year investigating the shadowy world of online scams, and how this global criminal industry is stealing billions of dollars each year. The 90-minute documentary “Scammed” goes inside the explosive growth of an industry powered in many cases by organized crime, trafficked labor, American technology, and, increasingly, AI — and how governments and law enforcement have tried to keep pace. 

Drawing on interviews with perpetrators, victims and officials, as well as thousands of never-before-seen documents, “Scammed” pieces together a look inside the global scam industry — from sextortion scams run from Nigeria, to massive scam compounds in Southeast Asia that rely on human trafficking for labor — and the underlying technologies and platforms being used to scam victims in the U.S. and worldwide. items.title: The Mysteries of Ancient Ireland | Full Series
items.author: History Hit
items.content:
<article>We explored the ancient sites of Ireland. 

Tristan Hughes explores the ancient myths that surround Stone Age Ireland and uncovers Ireland’s prehistoric metal revolution, the Bronze Age. 

In episode 1 Tristan visits the Brú na Bóinne complex, which holds some of the most extraordinary structures of the prehistoric world. Tristan travels to Ireland to delve into the mysteries of Newgrange and its surrounding tombs — exploring the secrets of Stone Age Ireland. Along the way, he gets up close to artefacts uncovered from the tombs, examines the breathtaking rock art carved into their stones, and investigates the myths and beliefs that have echoed through this sacred landscape for over 5,000 years.

A UNESCO World Heritage Site, Brú na Bóinne sits on the north bank of the River Boyne and is dominated by the world-famous passage tombs of Newgrange, Knowth, and Dowth. Older than the Great Pyramids of Giza, these monumental structures date back to the Neolithic Period, which began around 4000 BC. 

Newgrange has long been a centre of spiritual, astrological, and ceremonial significance — a sacred place where the natural world was revered and influential individuals were honoured in death.

In episode 2, Tristan traverses Ireland, exploring a golden age of transformation, Ireland’s Bronze Age. Copper mining started in Ireland around 2400 BC, in the Chalcolithic, or copper age, the period between the end of the Stone Age and the Bronze age. Tristan climbs Mount Gabriel in County Cork to investigate Bronze Age Copper mines. Ireland’s ‘copper craze’ continued for generations, but it wasn’t just copper that was found here, they also mined for gold! Tristan explores the beautifully intricate golden Lunula. Special boats and trackways appeared all over Ireland connecting these new bronze age billionaires to the wider prehistoric world. 

Tristan visits one of these trackways at Craggaunowen before getting hands on helping out with daily life. One of the most extraordinary legacies of Bronze Age Ireland are Fulacht Fiadh or burnt mounds, which are most probably ceremonial cooking sites, and Tristan gets to see one in action. But life in Bronze Age Ireland wasn’t all idyllic countryside cooking - by the middle of the Bronze Age defensive hillforts began to arise. Rathgall Hillfort epitomises this, it was a centre of defense, community, trade and the forging of weapons, tools and artefacts.

items.content:
<article>American soldiers stormed the beaches of Normandy on June 6th, 1944 and the nature of their mission meant that casualties would be piling up fast. Managing that situation would fall largely to combat medics who were rushed through training, parachuted into a war zone, targeted by enemy troops, and forced to work with whatever equipment they could find in the chaos of Omaha Beach  .

On this episode of Weird History, we take a look at what the D-Day invasion was like for the combat medics who ran headfirst into the most dangerous parts of the battle to save the wounded.

items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:

NotePin S: https://bit.ly/46IANlt

Amazon: https://amzn.to/4xFP79Q

Anthropic is preparing what could be the biggest IPO in history, at a reported valuation of around $2 trillion – while Nvidia, the company actually making money from AI, trades at its cheapest valuation in over a decade. In this video, finance professor Patrick Boyle looks at whether the AI boom is a bubble and what you would have to believe to pay $2 trillion for an AI lab. We cover the Anthropic and OpenAI IPO plans, why rising interest rates and a 5% ten-year Treasury yield are bad news for AI stocks, how "total addressable market" (TAM) estimates have been used to justify tech valuations from Amazon to Uber and WeWork, SoftBank's junk bonds and its $50 billion data-centre company SB Energy, the circular financing between Nvidia, OpenAI and SoftBank, and the AI price war with Chinese open-weight models like DeepSeek. Along the way, we revisit Scott McNealy's famous warning about Sun Microsystems and the dotcom bubble, and ask whether today's AI giants could turn out to be the Yahoo and Lycos of this era.

items.title: C++26 for Lazy Programmers • Will Briggs & Todd Montgomery • GOTO 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub
http://gotopia.tech/bookclub

Check out more here:
https://gotopia.tech/episodes/454

Will Briggs - Professor of Computer Science at University of Lynchburg & Author of "C++26 for Lazy Programmers"
Todd L. Montgomery - Software Professional & Advisor at DRW & Co-Author & Co-Maintainer of Aeron, Agrona & Simple Binary Encoding (SBE) 

RESOURCES
Will
https://www.linkedin.com/in/will-briggs-32635714a
https://www.lynchburg.edu/will-briggs

Todd
https://twitter.com/toddlmontgomery
https://www.linkedin.com/in/todd-montgomery-413a3216
https://github.com/tmontgomery

DESCRIPTION
Will Briggs — a University of Lynchburg computer science professor with three decades of experience teaching C++ — joins Todd L. Montgomery to talk through C++26 for Lazy Programmers, and the conversation opens on the question every language-learning book has to answer right now: does learning a language still matter when AI writes so much of the code?
Briggs' answer is refreshingly unhyped — he tests a new AI tool about once a year on a real, medium-difficulty problem, and as of this year's attempt, it still couldn't solve one, though it's genuinely useful for speeding up work he already understands. Both he and Montgomery land on the same practical conclusion: reading code fluently matters more now, not less, because code is increasingly how AI communicates back to you, and you can't debug or direct what you can't read. The rest of the conversation is a genuine craft discussion about how to teach C++ well — sequencing concepts so a beginner never has to hold two new ideas at once, giving double duty to topics like operator overloading and custom string classes, and deliberately introducing pointers nineteen chapters before ever using the word "pointer", by building the underlying mental model through arrays first.

For engineers who've been away from C++ or are watching it from a distance, there are a few sharp, specific takeaways: Briggs points to AI-generated C++ as noticeably more reliable than AI-generated Java, plausibly because of training-corpus quality rather than anything about the language itself, and he's blunt about C++26's biggest usability problem being proliferation, not power — he cites a case of 25 different ways floating around online just to initialize a single number, and argues the language needs fewer new ways to do old things. He also makes a case, backed by the TIOBE index, that C — a language from 1972 — is still the second most popular language in the world, and that learning C++ specifically (precisely because it's hard and concept-dense) is some of the best preparation available for picking up nearly any other language quickly afterward.

<article>Explore the physics of magnetism, and how its properties are used in modern technologies like MRI machines, hard drives, and more.

In the 1920s, physicists still had many unanswered questions about magnetism. items.title: What happens to these balloons when you open the valve?
items.author: Veritasium
items.content:
<article>Take a balloon and fill it with lots of air. Take another one and fill it with less air. Now connect the two via a valve. 

What do you think will happen when you open the valve?</article>
